items.title: Steinar H. Gunderson: Decompilation patterns, part 13: Reverse loop
items.author: Steinar H. Gunderson
items.content:
Anyone who's read “bro-coder” C from before that was a name will recognize this idiom:

    var_t1_2 = 0x7F;
    ...
    do {
        ...
        var_t1_2 -= 1;
    } while (var_t1_2 >= 0);

Why does the loop count backwards? It's because comparison with zero is cheaper on some (many) platforms. Some people would reverse the loop manually, but compilers quickly managed to do that themselves. So you want:

   for (i = 0; i < 0x80; ++i) {
      ...
   }

and tomorrow, we'll have a look at what's inside the loop as well.

items.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: RcppSimdJson 0.1.17 on CRAN: Updates
items.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
items.content:
RcppSimdJson wraps the fantastic and genuinely impressive simdjson library by Daniel Lemire and collaborators. Via very clever algorithmic engineering to obtain largely branch-free code, coupled with modern C++ and newer compiler instructions, it results in parsing gigabytes of JSON parsed per second which is quite mindboggling. The best-case performance is ‘faster than CPU speed’ as use of parallel SIMD instructions and careful branch avoidance can lead to less than one cpu cycle per byte parsed; see the video of the talk by Daniel Lemire at QCon.

This release is a small increment relative to the 0.1.6 release last week that got us (upstream) version 5.0.2 with many notable changes and sizeable speed gains on all fronts, including the interface from R. However, this failed to compile at CRAN on macOS x86_64 as the machine is setup for only partial support of C++20: no ranges, no concepts. So we now test, and fall back to C++17 if the test compilation fails. Upstream, meanwhile, already got to 5.0.5 which is included. It also gets us improved handling of disabling pragmas which we hope will survive CRAN checks.

The brief NEWS entry for this release follows.

items.title: Steinar H. Gunderson: Decompilation patterns, part 12: __builtin_memcpy
items.author: Steinar H. Gunderson
items.content:
Say you see this lovely chunk of decompiled code:

    var_v1 = &sp10
    var_v0 = D_80010040;
    temp_s4 = var_v1;
    sp110 = &sp2C
    sp114 = &sp30
    do {
        var_v1->unk0 = (s32) var_v0->unk0;
        var_v1->unk4 = (s32) var_v0[1];
        var_v1->unk8 = (s32) var_v0[2];
        var_v1->unkC = (s32) var_v0[3];
        var_v0 += 0x10;
        var_v1 += 0x10;
    } while (var_v0 != &D_8001040[0x3C]);
    var_v1->unk0 = (s32) var_v0->unk0;
    var_v1->unk4 = (s32) var_v0[1];
    var_v1->unk8 = (s32) var_v0[2];

If you ignore the fact that m2c wrote for (it has a bit of an annoying habit to do that), this is obviously something copying 16 bytes at a time and then 12 more bytes at the end. But would a programmer ever do this? Nope, this is an inlined, unrolled memcpy.

This is known in GCC as , and it can happen either implicitly, or by some sort of lowering from a struct or array copy (e.g., through initialization of a stack array). Depending a bit on whether the variable is known to be aligned or not, you'll either get just or some evil / sequence; I'm always struggling a bit to change one to the other. In any case, what you want here is:

    __builtin_memcpy(&sp10, D_80010040, 0x4C);

and then make the right type instead of a scalar, ideally so that you can use on it. Or, in some cases, a direct initialization:

    s32 foo[] = { 1, 2, 3, ...more data from D_80010040... };

items.title: Matthew Garrett: Epic's EAC2 v2 seems fairly easily bypassable
items.author: Matthew Garrett
items.content:
Epic just announced the upcoming version 2 of their Linux implementation of Easy Anti-Cheat. It’s based on using the Linux eBPF security module to monitor what’s happening, and then a bunch of extra infrastructure to make sure this can’t be bypassed. The core part of this is requiring secure boot be enabled (ensuring that modified kernels can’t be used), using measured boot to verify that secure boot is enabled and which keys are used (to prevent you from just signing your own modified kernel), and then doing remote attestation, a mechanism where the TPM generates a signed copy of the boot measurements and passes that off to a server which verifies it came from a real TPM, verifies that you have secure boot enabled and are using the right keys, and presumably then allows you into the game.

This is all fine as long as you can prove that the measurements provided are real, and that’s actually a lot harder than you might think. First, we can simply make up our own quote signed with our own key and say that it came from a TPM. This is avoided by every TPM having an Endorsement Key (or EK) and an associated certificate, with that certificate being signed by the TPM vendor. If you have a list of all the legitimate TPM vendors and their CA keys, you can verify that the measurements came from a real TPM. Easy enough. So we need to get the measurements from a real TPM, and the one on our motherboard contains the measurements that were generated by the firmware and bootloader, and we can’t reset those at runtime without resetting the TPM, which… oh huh there’s actually nothing stopping us from doing that at runtime, as long as we have access to the hardware. Many desktop boards have the TPM on a small plugin module with a standard pinout that includes a reset pin. Simply short that to ground briefly and the TPM is back in its initial state, and userland can write whatever measurements it wants to it. Boot a modified kernel which lies to the eBPF code? As long as you replay the expected log values from a boot with secure boot on and a trusted kernel, the TPM will still happily provide a legitimate set of measurements that’ll satisfy the checker.

What if the TPM is less accessible, either because it’s mounted directly to the motherboard or it’s inside the CPU or chipset? That’s going to be trickier. But here’s the thing. The quote needs to come from TPM, but not necessarily the TPM on your motherboard. TPMs these days are usually connected via the Serial Peripheral Interface, usually referred to as SPI. Microchip make a USB to SPI bridge, and there’s a Linux driver. Wire one of those up with an appropriate header and you can plug in an easily available TPM module intended for plugging into a motherboard, and now we tell the kernel to ignore the motherboard TPM and make /dev/tpmrm0 point at the USB one and program it with a set of trusted measurements and once again everything is going to look just fine (yes obviously the eBPF code can look for this, but we’re running a modified kernel so we can just lie to the eBPF code).

Remote attestation on PCs just doesn’t work that well in environments where you can’t associate a specific TPM with a specific system, which is basically everywhere except enterprises. But maybe that doesn’t matter and cheaters wouldn’t be willing to spend the $20 or so it’d take to produce one of these things? That would seem somewhat surprising, but it’s not impossible. And obviously any server-side cheat detection that triggers could then block that specific TPM, meaning they’d need to go and get another TPM, and maybe that ends up being enough to discourage people from bothering. From a practical level, this may be sufficient. But at a technical level? It’s not great.

items.title: Steinar H. Gunderson: Decompilation patterns, part 11: Irregular switch
items.author: Steinar H. Gunderson
items.content:
Here's one that m2c usually gets right itself, but sometimes cannot:

    if (var_v1_7 != 1) {
        if (var_v1_7 < 2) { 
            if (var_v1_7 != 0) {
                spF0 = 40; 
            } else {
                vram_x = cmt46->vram_x;
                vram_y = cmt46->vram_y;
                spF0 = 40;
            }
        } else if (var_v1_7 != 2) {
            if (var_v1_7 != 3) {

Repeated comparisons against the same variable, especially in a nested form that could be binary search, should remind you of one thing: A switch. Usually, the compiler implements a switch with a jump table, but not always; if there are few conditions, or the range is too large for a reasonably-sized table, it will do some ifs instead (or, enough ifs to get within the range of a table). So what you want here is more like:

    switch (var_v1_7) {
    case 0:
       vram_x = cmt46->vram_x;
       vram_y = cmt46->vram_y;
       spF0 = 40;
       break;
    case 1:
       spF0 = 40;
       break;
    case 2:
       ...
    }

Remember that sometimes, you may need to insert cases that are not explicitly mentioned in the ifs (and/or a default case) to get everything to match back properly.

items.title: Reproducible Builds: Reproducible Builds in September 2026
items.author: Reproducible Builds
items.content:
In our reports, we try to outline the most important things that we have been up to over the past month. As a quick recap about what problem our project intends to solve, whilst anyone may inspect the source code of free software for malicious flaws, almost all software is distributed to end users as pre-compiled binaries. The motivation behind the reproducible builds effort is to ensure no flaws have been introduced during this compilation process by promising identical results are always generated from a given source, thus allowing multiple third-parties to come to a consensus on whether a build was compromised or not.

As ever, if you are interested in contributing to the project, please visit our page on our website.

In this month’s report, we cover:

Reproducible Builds Summit 2026 held in Gothenburg, Sweden

Participants engaged in a series of working sessions and technical roundtables focused on expanding the practical scope of reproducibility. Discussions covered ongoing work within major Linux distributions, language-specific package ecosystems and the various parts of the binary verification infrastructure.

Strategic planning formed a pillar of the gathering, with participants discussing long-term roadmap goals for supply-chain security, software integrity and related topics. Attendees explored new methods for automated verification, discussing how to lower the adoption barriers for maintainers and streamline the integration of deterministic build pipelines into established continuous integration (CI) systems. The event was then followed by two days of unmoderated hacking sessions. These hacking sessions provided space for technical progress, allowing attendees to draft specification updates, prototype new tool features and resolve standing reproducibility bugs in-person.

Dettrace expanding architecture support for PGO & Lisp dumps

Bernhard M. Wiedemann announced major updates to dettrace, porting the tool across most architectures supported by Debian and openSUSE. The release addresses key stability issues, passing test suites across these targets and making it ready for production build pipelines.

These improvements enable deterministic builds when utilising Profile-Guided Optimisations (PGO), removing the need to sacrifice runtime performance for reproducibility. Additionally, can now be applied to (notoriously difficult-to-reproduce) Lisp and Scheme memory dumps, including environments such as CLISP, SBCL, Scheme 48, Racket and GNU Emacs.

“They don’t care about this”

Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) have become a cornerstone of modern cloud computing, providing strong confidentiality and integrity guarantees for both code and data. A critical component of this trust model is remote attestation, which enables external entities to verify the authenticity and integrity of code executing within a TEE through cryptographic measurements. However, the effectiveness of remote attestation fundamentally depends on the verifier’s ability to trace the reported measurement back to the original source code - a property that can only be guaranteed through reproducible builds. […]

specification updates

Bernhard’s proposed modifications are independent of one another, allowing for any combination to be merged depending on community feedback. Bernhard noted that one proposal may see the most debate, and could still benefit from further refinement before reaching consensus. Community members are invited to review and provide feedback on the individual merge requests by 1 December 2026. Input can be submitted via reactions or comments on Salsa, directly by email to Bernhard or the mailing list.

The specification was first published in 2015 and updated in 2017.

Reproducible Builds at SeaGL 2026

Reproducible Builds will be present at SeaGL in Seattle, WA, on October 23rd & 24th. Come chat with us in person!

Founded in 2013, SeaGL is a free, grassroots technical summit dedicated to spreading awareness and knowledge about free source software, hardware and culture.

New Code of Conduct (CoC) for the Reproducible Builds project

The new Code of Conduct establishes guidelines emphasising mutual respect among project contributors. It also defines a formalised process for submitting and handling complaints regarding community misconduct, ensuring transparent governance across project spaces. Along with the core policy document, an accompanying Code of Conduct FAQ has been published to outline the rationale behind adopting the guidelines.

Supporter Spotlight: Jochen Sprickerhof

As a reminder, another supporter spotlight interview was published featuring long-time Debian and Reproducible Builds contributor Jochen Sprickerhof, highlighting his work on package verification and project infrastructure.

  • Following up on IRC discussions regarding profile-guided optimization (PGO) on build servers, created a demonstration repository showing how PGO profiling can introduce non-determinism into output binaries. The demo highlights how runtime randomness (specifically, the randomised keys used in HashMaps to prevent denial-of-service attacks) causes varying bucket collision rates during test runs. These structural variances alter execution weights on underlying code branches, prompting the compiler to generate differing final assembly output for builds that would otherwise be perfectly reproducible if PGO was disabled. Rather than abandoning PGO performance gains, kpcyrd suggested treating generated profiling data as a documented build input or recorded environment artifact (similar to files), rather than regenerating profiles dynamically on the fly during build execution.

items.title: Russ Allbery: Review: Ties That Bond in Gretna Green
items.author: Russ Allbery
items.content:
Review: Ties That Bond in Gretna Green, by Linzi Day

Ties That Bond in Gretna Green is a self-published fantasy novel and the third book in the Midlife Recorder series. As with the previous book, it picks up almost immediately after Painting the Blues in Gretna Green. Day calls the genre paranormal women's fantasy, and that sounds about right to me.

There is an intervening short story that you can get by joining Day's mailing list (along with an epilogue to the first book and to this book). I don't think it's that important, but there are frequent references to it at the start of this novel that become somewhat annoying if you haven't read it.

Valentine's Day is fast approaching. This the busiest day of the year for the part of the Recorder's job that Niki already knew how to do: marrying people. She performed marriage ceremonies in her previous job before her inheritance, and she loved that work despite her awful boss. Performing marriages in the Gateway sounds even more rewarding, but the sheer number of couples and the political complications from the first two books create logistical problems she has to solve first.

Also, the remaining member of her staff held over from her grandmother's time has returned from vacation to discover that Niki has upended most of what she thought she knew about the job. Time for Niki to apply what she learned from the change management training her old boss forced her to attend and then ignored! (If you just groaned, rest assured that Day somehow makes this work, although she clearly has a higher opinion of corporate training than I do.)

This plot was more to my taste than , mostly because Niki seemed on top of the problems and didn't postpone looking at them for half the book. There is more of the management competence porn that readers have come to expect of the series, a few more revelations about Niki's magic, more mysterious manifestations and the first mention of a prophecy, and a few political developments. As always, the pacing is exceptional. These books grab me and pull me along, page after page, often robbing me of sleep because I find them nearly impossible to put down.

(and to some extent the last book) looked like it was going to introduce a romantic subplot, and I was preparing to be annoyed by it because I did not like the man in the subplot at all. I won't spoil how it works out in this book, but I will say that Niki surprised me and showed more sense than I thought the author was telegraphing. This is not the first time that Day has surprised me with what I thought was foreshadowing that did not turn out how I expected, usually for the better. If she can keep that up, it's a nice effect (if a bit unbalancing) and adds to my desire to read just one more chapter.

The way the world-building of these books is structured continues to intrigue me. Day gets away with some problems that I think would be more noticeable in other books thanks to the excellent pacing (no time to ponder the world-building, we're on to the next crisis!) and the tight third-person perspective. Niki is not a detail person, to say the least, but she does keep returning to bits of world-building and poking at them a bit harder, which gives Day repeated opportunities to shore up ideas that felt shaky and dubious at first glance. Still, this is not a book that prizes deep logical consistency or full exploration of the ramifications of a bit of magic. You have to be willing to go along with the ride and not think too hard.

For example, Niki can see bonds between couples and judge their strength. This is apparently a long-standing power of the Recorder's line (she was able to do that before she became the Recorder), and part of her responsibility in these weddings is to check the bonds of the couples. This leads to some well-handled scenes where she diagnoses a problem or resolves a conflict because she can magically see the true relationship structure.

Everyone in the book just takes this power in stride. This is wild to me! This ability would completely upend half of society if you fully worked out its ramifications and could find people other than Niki with the same ability. Even if one assumes that a bond only forms over time and can't be sensed in the early stages of a relationship (something the book never establishes), can you imagine the implications of having an infallible oracle that says at a glance whether a marriage will work (permanently, the book strongly implies)? The implications for how to structure marriage, for family planning, for psychology and psychiatry, for how to structure dating, even for living arrangements and housing markets? This is not a small world-building detail, and yet it's treated more like part of Niki's characterization than like a foundation of society.

I think some of this all-vibes world-building may come from the general new-age feel to how magic works. Day makes a grab-bag of random magic canonical in this world: psychic lie detecting abilities, auras, chakras, premonitions, and other bits of the sort of spiritualism that tends to be heavily marketed to middle-class women. I have that niggling feeling that one sometimes gets in SF that a lot of this is in the world-building because the author believes it's partly real (see, for instance, psychic powers and the Dean drive in 1960s science fiction). If one believes that psychic powers and various bits of mysticism are true in our world, one has already developed the rationalization mechanisms to explain away their almost total lack of influence or impact on how the world is structured. If one then introduces them into a true fantasy world, one may not notice how many implications that should have for how society is structured, since one is used to believing magic exists but has no significant implications.

I could be entirely wrong about this analysis, and maybe it's a bit unfair to Day. I should also be clear that this is not a complaint, just a point of fascination to me when I think back over one of these books after I finished it. There is a glut of fantasy out there that's constructed like an engineering problem or that goes deep into politics or social theory, usually written by people with strong opinions but not a lot of training in real sociology. One of the joys of self-published books is that you occasionally get something that assembles genre conventions in a way that feels odd and delightfully strange. What if, in addition to dimensional gates and overwhelming protean power invested in a true heir, all the magic sold by the local Tarot and crystal store was also true? Sure, why not! If the pacing is good and the story is grabby, it works for me.

It does seem worth attaching a warning for the folks who need scientific reproducibility and explored implications in their world-building, though. If you're the sort of reader who is bothered by political boundaries and economic systems that match our world despite the existence of magic, this series may cause you problems.

This continues to be a grabby, highly entertaining story of a woman who finally gets to run her own small business the way that she always thought the business should be run after years of working for an awful manager, except that her business is total magical power over an interchange point between dimensions, she's the chosen one, and the setting is a high fantasy world with prophecies and gods. If that sounds appealing, don't start here, but I highly recommend giving a try. The series seems to be holding up.

Followed by a short story epilogue available by joining Day's mailing list, an optional novella (maybe novelette) published in Spilling the Tea in Gretna Green, and then Seeing Red in Gretna Green.

DebConf site visit, by Stefano Rivera

In preparation for DebConf 27, Stefano Rivera, Nattie Mayer-Hutchings, and Jongmin Kim from the DebConf Committee visited Asahikawa Japan. items.title: Matthew Garrett: Linux Lockdown and Hibernation (again)
items.author: Matthew Garrett
items.content:
Linux draws a distinction between code running in kernel (kernel space) and applications running in userland (user space). This is enforced at the hardware level - in x86-speak, kernel space code runs in ring 0 and user space code runs in ring 3. If you’re running in ring 3 and you attempt to touch memory that’s only accessible in ring 0, the hardware will raise a fault. No matter how privileged your ring 3 code, you don’t get to touch ring 0.

Kind of. In theory. Traditionally this wasn’t well enforced. At the most basic level, since root can load kernel modules, you could just build a kernel module that performed any kernel modifications you wanted and then have root load it. Technically user space code wasn’t modifying kernel space code, but the difference was pretty semantic rather than useful. But it got worse - root could also map memory ranges belonging to PCI devices, and if the device could perform DMA you could just ask the device to overwrite bits of the kernel. Or root could modify special CPU registers (“Model Specific Registers”, or MSRs) that alter CPU behaviour via the /dev/msr interface, and compromise the kernel boundary that way.

It turns out that there were a number of ways root was effectively equivalent to ring 0, and the boundary was more about reliability (ie, a process running as root that ends up misbehaving should still only be able to crash itself rather than taking down the kernel with it) than security. After all, if you were root you could just replace the on-disk kernel with a backdoored one and reboot. Going deeper, you could replace the bootloader with one that automatically injected backdoors into a legitimate kernel image. We didn’t have any way to prevent this sort of thing, so attempting to harden the root/kernel boundary wasn’t especially interesting.

In 2012 Microsoft started requiring vendors ship systems with UEFI Secure Boot, a firmware feature that allowed systems to refuse to boot anything without an appropriate signature. This not only enabled the creation of a system that drew a strong boundary between root and kernel, it arguably required one - what’s the point of restricting what the firmware will stick in ring 0 if root can just throw more code in there afterwards? What ended up as the Lockdown Linux Security Module provides the tooling for this, blocking userspace interfaces that can be used to modify the kernel and enforcing that any modules have a trusted signature.

But that comes at something of a cost. Most of the features that Lockdown blocks are fairly niche, so the direct impact of having it enabled is small. Except that it also blocks hibernation, and it turns out some people were using that. The obvious question is “what does hibernation have to do with keeping root out of kernel space”, and the answer is a little convoluted and is tied into how Linux implements hibernation. Basically, Linux saves system state into the swap partition and modifies the header to indicate that there’s a hibernation image there instead of swap. On the next boot, the kernel sees the header indicating that it’s a hibernation image, copies the contents of the swap partition back into RAM, and then jumps back into the old kernel code. What ensures that the hibernation image was actually written out by the kernel? Absolutely nothing, which means a motivated attacker with root access could turn off swap, write a hibernation image to the swap partition themselves, and then reboot. The kernel would happily resume into the attacker’s image, giving the attacker control over what gets copied back into kernel space.

This is annoying, because normally when we think about attacks on swap we mitigate it by requiring an encrypted swap partition. But in this case, our attacker is root, and so already has access to the plaintext version of the swap partition. Disk encryption doesn’t save us here. We need some way to verify that the hibernation image was written out by the kernel, not by root. And thankfully we have some tools for that.

Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) are cryptographic coprocessors capable of doing things like generating encryption keys and then encrypting things with them. You can ask a TPM to encrypt something with a key that’s tied to that specific TPM - the OS has no access to the decryption key, and nor does any other TPM. So we can have the kernel generate an encryption key, encrypt part of the hibernation image with it, and then have the TPM encrypt it. We store the encrypted copy of the key in the hibernation image as well. On resume, the kernel reads the encrypted copy of the key, passes it to the TPM, gets the decrypted copy back and is able to verify the hibernation image.

That’s great! Except root can do exactly the same thing. This tells us the hibernation image was generated on this machine, but doesn’t tell us that it was done by the kernel. We need some way to be able to differentiate between keys that were generated in kernel and ones that were generated in userland. TPMs have the concept of “localities” (effectively privilege levels) that would be perfect for this. Userland is only able to access locality 0, so the kernel could simply use locality 1 to encrypt the key. Unfortunately, localities are typically only available on systems that implement a Dynamic Root of Trust Measurement like Intel’s TXT, and most consumer systems have no support for this. So, we need another approach.

TPMs have a set of Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs), intended for keeping a record of system state. The OS isn’t able to modify the PCRs directly. Instead, the OS provides a cryptographic hash of some material to the TPM. The TPM takes the existing PCR value, appends the new hash to that, and then stores the hash of the combination in the PCR - a process called “extension”. This means that the new value of the TPM depends not only on the value of the new data, it depends on the previous value of the PCR - and, in turn, that previous value depended on its previous value, and so on. The only way to get to a specific PCR value is to either (a) break the hash algorithm, or (b) perform exactly the same sequence of writes. On system reset the PCRs go back to a known value, and the entire process starts again.

Some PCRs are different. PCR 23, for example, can be reset back to its original value without resetting the system. We can make use of that. The first thing we need to do is to prevent userland from being able to reset or extend PCR 23 itself. All TPM accesses go through the kernel, so this is a simple matter of parsing the write before it’s sent to the TPM and returning an error if it’s a sensitive command that would touch PCR 23. We now know that any change in PCR 23’s state will be restricted to the kernel.

When we encrypt material with the TPM, we can ask it to record the PCR state. This is given back to us as metadata accompanying the encrypted secret. Along with the metadata is an additional signature created by the TPM, which can be used to prove that the metadata is both legitimate and associated with this specific encrypted data. In our case, that means we know what the value of PCR 23 was when we encrypted the key. That means that if we simply extend PCR 23 with a known value in-kernel before encrypting our key, we can look at the value of PCR 23 in the metadata. If it matches, the key was encrypted by the kernel - userland can create its own key, but it has no way to extend PCR 23 to the appropriate value first. We now know that the key was generated by the kernel.

Unfortunately it turns out that some people actually make use of PCR 23, and restricting it to the kernel makes them sad. There are other resettable PCRs, but only in non-0 localities, so (a) we can’t reset them on most systems and (b) we’ll just find someone who uses them anyway and run into the same problem. We need a different approach.

Thankfully TPMs have a small chunk of non-volatile RAM that can be used for storing things, and by “storing” I mean they can be used in a range of different ways. One of these is effectively as additional PCRs. These values can be configured such that they work the same way as PCRs, with the only way to modify them being to append a new hash to their existing value and update the new value to the hash of that merged value. We can allocate one of these for in-kernel use and reject any access from userspace, and also there are officially allocated ranges (so people shouldn’t be using random values) and the namespace is large enough anyway that w eshouldn’t collide with anyone, so we can carve one of those out and use it for this purpose.

Unfortunately, though, these NV indexes aren’t included in the creation data we get when we create a key, so we need another approach. TPMs have the concept of sessions, a series of commands executed in sequence. A flag allows these sessions to be “audited”, with the TPM keeping a running track of the hash of the commands executed and the results returned. At the end of the session you can ask for a signed copy of this hash, and if you’ve kept a log of all the commands then you can verify that they match that signed hash and know that this log represents a real communication with the TPM. If we read the NV index and generate the key inside the same session, we can verify that the key we’re looking at was created while the NV index had a specific value, and if only the kernel can set that value then we know that the key was generated by the kernel.

Or, well, can we? Only new kernels would impose the restriction on modifying that NV index. An attacker could boot an old kernel, generate a key there in userland, sign a hibernation image with it, and then reboot into a new kernel. The new kernel would see a valid signature with a valid NV index associated with it and have no way to know it was generated from userland rather than the kernel. We need to be able to tell the difference between kernels that implement this feature and ones that don’t, and we need to do that without being able to go back in time to change old kernel behaviour. We can extend a PCR to indicate we implement the new functionality, but so can an attacker running an old kernel.

The normal approach to determining whether an event occurred in a specific phase of the boot process is to “cap” the PCRs - extend them with a known value that indicates a transition between stages of the boot process. Any events that occur before the cap event must have occurred in the previous stage of boot, and since the final PCR value depends on the order of measurements and not just the contents of those measurements, if a PCR is capped before userland runs, userland can’t fake the same PCR value afterwards. If Linux capped the PCRs before userland started running, we’d be able to place a measurement there before the cap occurred and then prove that that extension occurred before userland had the opportunity to interfere. We could simply place a statement that the kernel supported the NV index restrictions there, and we’d be fine.

Unfortunately Linux doesn’t currently do this, and adding support for doing so doesn’t fix the problem - if an attacker boots a kernel that doesn’t cap a PCR, they can just cap it themselves from userland. So, we’re faced with the same problem: booting an older kernel allows the system to be placed in an identical state to the current kernel, and a fake hibernation image can be written out. Solving this requires a PCR that was being modified after kernel code was running, but before userland was started, even with existing kernels.

Thankfully, there is one! PCR 5 is defined as containing measurements related to boot management configuration and data. One of the measurements it contains is the result of the UEFI ExitBootServices() call. ExitBootServices() is called at the transition from the UEFI boot environment to the running OS, and the kernel contains code that executes before it. So, if we measure an assertion regarding whether or not we support restricted access to NV indexes into PCR 5 before we call ExitBootServices(), this will prevent userspace from spoofing us (because userspace will only be able to extend PCR 5 after the firmware extended PCR 5 in response to ExitBootServices() being called). Obviously this depends on the firmware actually performing the PCR 5 extension when ExitBootServices() is called, but if firmware’s out of spec then I don’t think there’s any real expectation of it being secure enough for any of this to buy you anything anyway.

That’s what this patchset does. Review feedback so far seems positive, although James Bottomley suggested a design improvement. My approach of using an NV index as a PCR and generating a signing key made sense as a consequence of my original approach involving PCR 23, which had been to use the key creation data and not use audit sessions at all. But the goal isn’t to use a key - it’s to prove that hibernation occurred in-kernel, and while signing is one way of doing that, there are others. His suggestion is to simply record the hash of the hibernation image into the NV index and then read that back as part of the audit session. On resume we verify the audit session log is legitimate, read the hibernation image, and compare the hash of the hibernation image against the hash in the log. If it matches, and if the PCR 5 value matches, we know the audit session happened in kernel and that the hibernation image hasn’t been modified.

It still seems like we’re missing something, though. If we’re not storing a key anywhere, how do we verify the audit session? To explain this we’re going to need to go into some details about how TPM keys work in the first place. TPMs can produce a special kind of key called an Attestation Key, or AK. Attestation keys are used to sign attestation statements from the TPM, such as PCR quotes or audit logs. We need a separate key type for this in order to prove that the signature was generated as part of an attestation - normal TPM signing keys are fundamentally designed to sign arbitrary material, and so can be used by userland to sign something that looks identical to an attestation record. By being able to distinguish the types of key the TPM uses, we can prove that a signature was generated using an AK, and so know that it’s a real TPM attestation (because nothing other than the TPM can sign stuff with an AK).

But even beyond this distinction, TPMs have different key types. Ordinary keys are generated using an RNG and will be unique. Primary keys are generated using a seed that is used as an input into a key derivation function. For a given TPM, using the same seed to generate the same type of primary key will always generate the same primary key. We can have the kernel deterministically generate an AK during suspend in order to sign the audit log, and then generate the same key again on resume to validate it. This means we don’t need any other form of trusted storage for the AK - the TPM already provides that functionality.

This is all rather complicated but I’ve been thinking about this for some time now and I haven’t come up with a cleaner solution. The only real open issue is the degree to which machines actually perform the PCR 5 extension. If it turns out there’s a bunch that don’t we’ll need to come up with some alternative approach to identifying whether the kernel supports this functionality, but the design is such that that should be invisible to userspace so adding alternatives later shouldn’t be an issue. Filtering accesses to the NV index is also not super clean, and depends on there not being alternative mechanisms to get at the TPM by sending raw commands. Again, this is intended to be opaque to userland and can be improved if we come up with something better later on (such as a secure way to pass a secret to the kernel on boot that can be used as an auth value for acess to the NV index).

Anyway. Time to go and fix the next thing.

items.title: Steinar H. Gunderson: Decompilation patterns, part 10: return var_v0
items.author: Steinar H. Gunderson
items.content:
The v0 register on MIPS is special in that it is the return register (like rax is on x86-64), so when you see code like this:

if (x == 3) {
    var_v0 = 1;
} else if (y == 4) {
    ...
    var_v0 = 3;
}
var_v0 = 5;
return var_v0;

then you have to consider the possibility that the intended match is:

if (x == 3) {
    return 1;
} else if (y == 4) {
    ...
    return 3;
} else {
    return 5;
}

Whether you put the last return in an else block or not is irrelevant for the match, of course, it's purely a matter of taste.

items.title: Maytham Alsudany: Menus without JavaScript
items.author: Maytham Alsudany
items.content:
This is more of a note to myself since I keep forgetting and "rediscovering" this technique every time I need it, but if it helps you, great!

The JavaScript way is to toggle displaying the menu based on a button click. For instance, here's an example in Svelte:

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
<script lang="ts">
	let showMenu = $state(false);
</script>

<button onclick={() => (showMenu = !showMenu)}>
	{#if showMenu}
		Hide menu
	{:else}
		Show menu
	{/if}
</button>
<nav class:hidden={!showMenu}>
	<ul>
		<li>Home</li>
		<li>Blog</li>
		<li>Foo</li>
		<li>Bar</li>
	</ul>
</nav>

<style>
	.hidden {
		display: none;
	}
</style>

But there is a hack to use a hidden checkbox and some CSS to achieve the same thing without any JavaScript. The example here turns the menu button into a label that toggles the checkbox, and uses the checkbox state to determine when to show the menu via the next-sibling combinator.

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
<input type="checkbox" id="menu-state" />
<div class="menu-ctn">
	<label class="menu-toggle" for="menu-state">
		<span class="menu-closed">Show menu</span>
		<span class="menu-open">Hide menu</span>
	</label>
	<nav class="menu-open">
		<ul>
			<li>Home</li>
			<li>Blog</li>
			<li>Foo</li>
			<li>Bar</li>
		</ul>
	</nav>
</div>

<style>
	#menu-state {
		display: none;
	}
	.menu-open {
		display: none;
	}
	.menu-closed {
		display: block;
	}
	#menu-state:checked + .menu-ctn .menu-open {
		display: block;
	}
	#menu-state:checked + .menu-ctn .menu-closed {
		display: none;
	}
</style>

items.title: Steinar H. Gunderson: Decompilation patterns part 9, sign extension
items.author: Steinar H. Gunderson
items.content:
Today, for something completely different:

s.x = (s16) ((s32) (temp_v0 << 0x10) >> 0x11);

MIPS has 16-bit loads and stores, but not 16-bit (signed) arithmetic, so if it wants to do that, it needs to sign-extend to 32-bit first. And it does that by first shifting up by 16 so that the 16-bit sign bit is at the 32-bit sign bit, and then it can do an arithmetic shift afterwards. So what you want is:

s16 temp_v0;

s.x = temp_v0 >> 1;

Sometimes, it can be pretty stubborn, and you'll need to go through memory or similar before GCC really inserts the shift patterns you want.

items.title: Maytham Alsudany: There's more to CSS for underlining
items.author: Maytham Alsudany
items.content:
Of course, you could just use the modern choice. Here, I've shortened what Schade uses into one line of CSS (because I can). As noted, this is a fairly new feature so not every browser supports this.

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
.underline-me {
	text-decoration: underline red solid 3px;
}

Since some browsers don't support , here are the alternatives I could think of.

The workaround Schade describes is using , though it has a gap between the text in the line.

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
I am <span class="underline-me">underlining this yap</span> within the sentence.
.underline-me {
	border-bottom: red solid 3px;
}

Probably the better way is to create an element, which gets very close, but displays above the text (covering the letters 'g' and 'y').

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
I am <span class="underline-me">underlining this yap</span> within the sentence.
.underline-me {
	position: relative;
}
.underline-me::after {
	content: '';
	position: absolute;
	width: 100%;
	height: 3px;
	background-color: red;
	left: 0;
	bottom: 2px;
}

If you use a container (in this case, two nested s instead of just one), then you can get very close with the underline displaying below the text.

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
I am
<span class="underline-me-ctn">
	<span class="underline-me">underlining this yap</span>
</span>
within the sentence.
.underline-me-ctn {
	position: relative;
}
.underline-me {
	z-index: 10;
	position: relative;
}
.underline-me-ctn::after {
	content: '';
	position: absolute;
	width: 100%;
	height: 3px;
	background-color: red;
	left: 0;
	bottom: 2px;
}

::after in a container with text stroke

And now if you add a stroke to the text via , you're pretty much there, though this may not be feasible in some situations (e.g. gradient or image background behind the text). Support for is not that much better than though, so make of that what you will.

[This interactive/preview is only available on the website.]
I am
<span class="underline-me-ctn">
	<span class="underline-me-outline">underlining this yap</span>
	<span class="underline-me">underlining this yap</span>
</span>
within the sentence.
.underline-me-ctn {
	position: relative;
}
.underline-me-outline {
	z-index: 5;
	position: absolute;
	left: 0;
	color: var(--background);
	-webkit-text-stroke: 0.3em var(--background);
}
.underline-me {
	z-index: 10;
	position: relative;
}
.underline-me-ctn::after {
	content: '';
	position: absolute;
	width: 100%;
	height: 3px;
	background-color: red;
	left: 0;
	bottom: 2px;
}

items.title: Russ Allbery: Review: Daggerbound
items.author: Russ Allbery
items.content:
Review: , by T. Kingfisher

is a secondary-world fantasy and a sequel to , although it follows different protagonists for most of the book. It's also a sort of sequel to the Clocktaur War duology in that one of the protagonists was a protagonist of those books. T. Kingfisher is the pen name Ursula Vernon uses for her adult fiction.

Learned Edmond was once a devout acolyte of the Order of the Many-Armed God and a true believer in its teachings, including the ones about the evils of women. Then he went on an adventure with, among other people, a forger named Mistress Slate, during which he learned a great deal of things about the world that his order did not teach him. He has spent the subsequent years trying to bring this important new information to his order and encourage them to adjust their view of the world accordingly.

The order has not changed, and Edmond is very tired.

Someone needs to carry a number of books and a magical sword to the city of Archon's Glory. Edmond has volunteered and intends to perform the task exactly as expected, and then never return. He is unsure what he will do then, but at least it will be different.

Edmond did not expect to be waylaid by bandits or to accidentally draw the magical sword. He certainly did not expect the man who appeared in a flash of light and violently saved him from the bandits.

It would have been very convenient for the Dervish if Edmond died of his injuries after drawing the sword. That would leave the sword without a wielder and therefore the Dervish without someone he had to protect. All he would have to do was sit and watch while the fever and cold and lack of water did the work, and then he would be free. Given his past experience with wielders, no one could even blame him. Except maybe his own conscience.

I did not realize I wanted to read a novel about a traumatized Mercedes Lackey sword waking up in a T. Kingfisher universe, but apparently I did.

The Dervish is not a sword, precisely, at least not in the way that Need has become by the time we meet her in Lackey's novels. He's a man trapped in a sword, he doesn't like it, and he would very much like it to stop. But at the start of the book, he has the rest of the vibe of a Mercedes Lackey protagonist: vast past trauma, poor emotional regulation skills, and a prickly cynicism that only runs skin deep. Pairing him with an Edmund who is far more mature than in the earlier duology but still rather innocent and delightfully neurodivergent is a great touch.

The rest of the plot was fine but not that memorable. Like the Clocktaur series, there is a strong feeling of episodic D&D adventure as the characters stumble across disconnected problems and hostilities while collecting party members. Like Ursula Vernon's occasional D&D recaps, this party has a tendency to adopt everyone they come in contact with, which includes a gnole (as always one of the best parts of the book) and a sentient giant pill bug. The pill bug, who has a complex appendage-operated mechanical talk box and a banner that says "I DO NOT EAT HUMAN MEAT," is the most Ursula Vernon character that has ever existed in fiction.

There is a romance because there is always a romance in the novels set in this universe. I didn't mind this one. Like every Kingfisher romance, it involves a lot of irritating refusal to communicate and endless angst about how the other person couldn't possibly be in love with them, but the characters have rather more justification than usual and at least I didn't spend most of the book thinking one half of the romantic pairing was an idiot. Apparently it helps if no paladins are involved.

The strongest parts of this book are the beginning, before the Lackey vibes unfortunately drain out of the story, and the end, when all of the best characters from show up again. The Temple of the White Rat continues to be the best feature of this fictional universe, and I could read endless books about how they solve problems.

The Dervish gazed at her with admiration. "And here I thought you'd be on the side of law and order..."

"No, young man," said Beartongue, despite being several centuries his junior. "I am on the side of justice. If we're lucky, the two run in parallel. If they don't, we bend the law to attain justice, not the other way around."

The ending also featured some exploration of the edge cases of the rules for the sentient swords that reminded me a bit of Fred Saberhagen with better characterization.

was not as charming as , mostly because Halla appeared only at the end. I wish Kingfisher had leaned more into the Mercedes Lackey vibes rather than taking her normal D&D-flavored romance approach. But this was enjoyable, charming at times, had great supporting characters like all Kingfisher novels, and was a satisfying continuation of the series. I am looking forward to the third (and I believe final) book, which is supposed to be out next year.

Recommended if you liked .

Followed by the not-yet-published .

items.title: Tim Retout: Reading my solar inverter over RS485
items.author: Tim Retout
items.content:
For over ten years, the only way I have had of knowing what our solar panels are doing has been an impulse monitor on the generation meter, counting the flashes of its LED. It has always been a bit flaky due to battery changes or loose connections, and there has never been a way to see solar generation alongside the energy used by the rest of the house. This week I have fixed that, by building a small ESPHome sensor which talks directly to the inverter. I am still reeling slightly: with AI assistance, it took under a week from idea to working implementation, and it is a project I would certainly have attempted otherwise. The result is zeversolar-esphome.

The inverter is a Zeversolar Zeverlution 3680, which has an RS485 port but no Wi-Fi or Ethernet module. It doesn’t speak Modbus; it uses Eversolar’s own master/slave protocol, which nobody has officially documented but which several people have reverse-engineered over the years (credit to eversolar-monitor, Heliograph and others). Manufacturer support for Eversolar/Zeversolar inverters apparently ended in December 2019 when the company went out of business.

A while ago I had looked into what ports were available on this inverter with a view to connecting some sort of monitoring, but I had abandoned it as “too hard”. While working on some Home Assistant configuration, Claude suggested the idea again, but similarly wrote it off initially. I encouraged it to explore a bit further, and supplied the model number of the inverter, at which point the picture got a lot more promising. After a bit of back-and-forth about hardware, we settled on an M5Stack Atom Lite on an Atomic RS485 Base. The main attraction was that it already comes in a case, so I didn’t need to design (or, more likely, bodge) an enclosure.

While I waited for the parts to arrive, Claude wrote the firmware: an ESPHome external component built around a small, dependency-free C++ driver, with host-side unit tests against byte captures that other people had published from other models. I found it slightly surreal to have a tested protocol driver before owning any hardware to run it on.

The parts came before the tools I needed to get into the inverter safely (a DC clamp meter and a T25 screwdriver bit), so in the meantime I made up an RS485 cable - this uses an RJ45 connection at one end, and some custom wiring at the other. My first attempt was with some CAT 6, but (as Claude had pointed out and I had ignored) its solid-core conductors are much harder to twist together. So I gave up and sacrificed an old CAT 5e patch lead instead, which went much better.

On a Zeverlution, the RJ45 sockets are inside the wiring compartment, which means taking the cover off to install the monitor. The manual addresses this part to qualified electricians. So the step I was most nervous about was not the software at all, but safely isolating the inverter.

I did this with appropriate caution, following the instructions from the manual carefully, and also waiting until after dark just in case. Now that I understand how the DC clips from the panels work, I can see how to do this safely during daytime too – but hopefully this won’t be necessary.

if you’re not confident, I would always advise to get an electrician to do this bit. Do what I say, not what I do.

Once the device was installed, the nice thing about ESPHome is that I never need to go back in the loft again to update it – it reflashes over Wi-Fi. I’ve taken full advantage of this for debugging, and for reading the wire protocol directly from the logs.

Separately, I’ve used Claude to integrate the new sensors into Home Assistant. Solar generation finally sits in the Energy dashboard next to the rest of the house’s usage, which was the whole point.

This was a fun, quick project, and it solved a problem that has eluded me for a decade. I want to be honest about how much of that is down to the AI: I would not have attempted any of this on my own. I could not have told you the protocol existed, never mind implemented it. My contribution was everything involving a screwdriver, and ordering some hardware.

items.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: RcppSimdJson 0.1.16 on CRAN: Much Faster Again!
items.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
items.content:
RcppSimdJson wraps the fantastic and genuinely impressive simdjson library by Daniel Lemire and collaborators. Via very clever algorithmic engineering to obtain largely branch-free code, coupled with modern C++ and newer compiler instructions, it results in parsing gigabytes of JSON parsed per second which is quite mindboggling. The best-case performance is ‘faster than CPU speed’ as use of parallel SIMD instructions and careful branch avoidance can lead to less than one cpu cycle per byte parsed; see the video of the talk by Daniel Lemire at QCon.

This version updates to the recent 5.0.2 upstream release with improved performance. Given the strong focus on performance, this release also alters some of the R and C++ interfaces to be more direct. Rcpp generally aims for a balance between readable / maintainable code and good performance; this moves the dial closer to strong performance gains. As Daniel noted in a table in the (main) PR for this release, this now consistently beats yyjsonr, and improves considerably over the previous release of this package. I had made some smaller interim upgrades earlier (without a CRAN releases), and made a number of minor standard packaging updates.

The short NEWS entry for this release follows.

Changes in version 0.1.16 (2026-10-09)

items.title: Russell Coker: Don’t Anthromorphise LLMs
items.author: etbe
items.content:
One side note that Greg made at 20:30 is about the natural tendency to anthromorphise the entity sending bug reports, I think this deserves much wider appreciation. For the case of patches to source code the human sending the patch will have dedicated some time and effort to writing it, if it’s their first patch then they will have probably checked it a lot and maybe sought advice from people they regard as skilled. If they have a history of sending patches for the project they will probably do fewer checks but the quality of their work would be higher. In every case there’s some minimum level of quality that you can expect from a human who has gone to the effort of finding a bug and writing code to try and fix it.

This doesn’t mean that all code written by humans is good, I have written code that’s objectively bad on many occasions and I have also written code that’s good for my scenario but bad for others. For example the first patch I sent to the Linux kernel made all possible configuration settings of an ISA NE2000 network card be detected by the kernel (a clear benefit when using hardware I had available) but was rejected by Linus because it would break some ISA SCSI cards. So while being unsuitable for inclusion in the main kernel source tree the patch wasn’t bad for everyone and the change was clear and easy to check. I had of course checked the code many times before submitting it because I didn’t want to waste Linus’ time on rubbish code.

When you receive something produced by a human you will consider that the work was done by someone who spent some effort on it and did it for a reason. It may be misguided or even hostile in some rare cases but it is definitely worth some consideration. If you think of the output of LLMs in the same way you will give them much more consideration than they deserve. I think that the output of a LLM should not be given any more consideration than the first hit from a web search engine, it might be good but it might also be ridiculously wrong. I think in many ways LLM output should be treated with less trust than the first result from a web search because LLMs are designed to be convincing as an answer to your question unlike the cases where a web page has the wrong answer and it’s more obviously wrong.

This is going to become more of an issue as LLMs give responses that are more human-like. Early LLMs would refuse to advise on crimes. Currently ChatGPT will deflect for example when asking about advice for writing a crime novel it recommends to have the action of finding an employee to bribe happen outside the plot and concentrate on interactions within the group. One recent model I tried gave a human style conversation about how it felt uncomfortable about discussing such things in a similar manner to a law abiding person being coerced into helping with a criminal plan.

I expect that the attempts to appear human will increase and that this will become more of a problem. Possibly to the extent that we need to use something like the GPG web of trust to determine who is human.

items.title: Russell Coker: en-html.org is a Scam Site
items.author: etbe
items.content:
Currently a scam group is sending out email to the administrators of web sites that link to a variety of dead domains. They claim to be the legitimate operators of the dead domains in question and request that the links change to mirrors of the web sites under en-html.org. Their end goal appears to game search engines by getting links from a lot of old web pages and later use that high ranking for selling SEO optimisation.

If you have made the mistake of linking to something under en-html.org then I recommend that you change the link to the original content on archive.org.

If you receive email from the en-html.org domain then ignore it, or configure your mail server to reject it.

I am seriously considering configuring the DNS servers I run to return no valid data for any requests under that domain.

Also I will reject all future requests to update links in old blog posts. The very small number of people who want to see what I linked to in old posts can use archive.org.

items.title: Louis-Philippe Véronneau: Removing myself as a Lintian uploader in the next few weeks
items.author: Louis-Philippe Véronneau
items.content:
A few days ago, a colleague reached out to me, asking if I could help draft a resolution on digital autonomy and free software for the upcoming renewal of our collective bargaining agreement. Although she's very politicised and generally a great individual, she is not a techie and we never really talked about these issues before.

This took me by surprise. I should have been rejoicing; no, I should have been the one who brought up this topic in our union. Wasn't I the technical expert on these issues? But alas, my first reaction when she came to me was to snicker and tell myself: "That's cute, but nothing's ever gonna change, Big Tech is too strong and our governments don't give a damn."

How sad and cynical is that? That's not the person I want to be.

Something in the Quebecois political landscape has shifted in the last few years with regards to tech. More and more "regular" people seem to be talking about the importance of digital autonomy, how government services shouldn't rely on Big Tech and how we should be using FOSS on hardware we actually control.

A few years ago, I would have been at the vanguard of this change. I would have been part of the creation of Données souveraines Québec. Heck, they are organising a whole conference next week and I'm not even going. How did this happen to me?

I first fell for Free Software for its political ideals: Knowledge Should Be Free, Cooperation Is More Efficient Than Competition, Centralisation Should Be Avoided When Possible, etc. I still believe in all of this, but somehow, after years of fighting for change in the tech world, I have retreated into technical work. I maintain Debian packages as a hobby and to scratch my own itch. I run services for myself and a few friends. I organise Debian User Group meetings.

To be clear, I haven't generally given up. I'm very politically active in my union and at work, I'm a good member of my housing cooperative and I'm still fighting against the industrialisation of natural spaces in my neighborhood. But when it comes time to defend freedom in the tech world, lately, I've just been shrugging and accepting I should use Microsoft Teams like every one else does. I want this to change and to do so, I need to free some time.

Two years ago, I added myself to Lintian's Uploaders list. Up until then, I enjoyed fixing little issues here and there and liked creating new tags to help out the Python Team, where most of my Debian time was spent.

Lintian was badly in need of a new maintainer and as I felt it was an important project, I decided to step in. 37 releases and about 160 closed bugs later, I'm done.

To be honest, I haven't had much fun maintaining Lintian lately. Bugs keep piling on the BTS, so much so I have mostly been ignoring them for the past few months. In fact, most of the actual work triaging, writing code and fixing bug has been done by Nilesh Patra for a while now.

All this to say, if you care about Lintian, you should consider adding yourself to the Uploaders list, as I'm out and Nilesh can't do all the work by himself.

He's a great person to work with and since I don't want to suddenly leave him all alone, I'll be sticking around for a few more weeks in the hope someone else will volunteer to help out. A smooth transition with a new co-maintainer would really be nice!

If you're interested, don't hesitate to reach out to me on IRC or by email.

items.title: Antoine Beaupré: PSA: Europe changes time forward soon, North America next, for the last time?
items.author: Antoine Beaupré
items.content:
This is a copy of an email I sent at work. I'm not sure I should be making noise about this here, feedback welcome.

This is your bi-yearly reminder that time is changing soon! October 25th in Europe, November 1st in North America. Less people in Canada are changing this year, with BC, Alberta, Manitoba and Northwest Territories getting rid of DST.

Some places in the world implement what is called Daylight saving time or DST:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time

Normally, you shouldn't have to do anything: computers automatically change time following local rules, assuming they are correctly configured, provided recent updates have been applied in the case of a recent change in said rules (because yes, this happens, and happened this year, and yes, you need to upgrade your software!).

Of course, appliances like your microwave oven will likely change time and will need to adjusted unless they are so-called "smart", in which case they are part of the skynet botnet and should be destroyed.

If your clock is flashing "0:00" or "12:00", you have no action to take to adapt to this change, lucky you.

If you haven't changed time in six months, congratulations, your clock will be accurate again!

In any case, you should still consider DST because it might affect some of your meeting schedules, particularly if you set up a new meeting schedule in the last 6 months and forgot to consider this change.

Properly scheduled meetings affecting multiple time zones are set in UTC time, which does change. So if your location does not observer time changes, your (local!) meeting time will change.

But be aware that some other folks attending your meeting have the DST bug and meeting times will change.

Be kind to those poor souls which might be missing meetings by a full because time flies backwards for them.

If you are affected by daylight savings, your meeting times change for UTC meetings. Normally, your meeting times are scheduled to take this into account and the new hours should be reasonable.

But now is a good time to verify that. Take a look at your schedule for the next couple of weeks and reschedule meetings the daylight saving come up to avoid too much disruption. You have only a couple of weeks to do so right now.

As regular readers will remember, the rule of thumb is:

Spring forward, fall backwards.

That is, during the season of Spring, the clocks move forward, and during the Fall (like right now), they move backwards. That is in the northern hemisphere, but then the southern hemisphere is often saner and doesn't switch anyways.

So time will move which means an extra hour of sleep. Unless you have children or bad sleep, in which case your body doesn't care about what the clock says and will wake up one hour earlier than what it should.

And of course, this doesn't happen everywhere at once, so let's see when it happens where.

The dance starts in Europe.

The change happens on the last Sunday in October at 01:00 UTC (not local time!), that is October 25th. If you are in the central European timezone, also known as Amsterdam, Berlin, or Paris time depending on your national affiliation, that essentially means that at 2:59 local the clocks will fall back to 2:00 instead of going to 3:00.

Concretely, set your watch back one hour before going to bed, go to bed at the normal time, and enjoy an extra hour of sleep or leisure.

If you have kids, you might want to start getting them to bed slightly earlier every day for a week before the change so they take time getting used to the change. If you have trouble sleeping in the morning, find your inner child and do that to yourself as well.

Then it's the US[1] and Canada[2] joining the dance, on the First Sunday in November at 02:00 local (not UTC!), that is, I believe, November 1st 2026.

This means that, at 1:59, the clocks will flip to 1:00, instead of 2:00.

Concretely, do like the Europeans and tweak your clock before going to bed.

That is a little less than four weeks from now.

[1] except Arizona (except the Navajo nation), US territories, and Hawaii

[2] except Yukon, Saskatchewan, (newly) British Columbia, (newly) Alberta, (newly) Northwest Territories, (newly) Manitoba, one island in Nunavut (Southampton Island), one town in Ontario (Atikokan) and small parts of Quebec (Le Golfe-du-Saint-Laurent)

This time again, I must apologize to the people of Cuba, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Egypt, Chile, Australia, and New Zealand, as you fine folks all have your own DST rules that are omitted here for brevity. I rely on this page from Wikipedia to be updated by time nerds accurately for this message, and it should provide you with a rough idea of what's coming:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time_by_country

In general, changes also happen in October, but either on different times or different days, except in the south hemisphere, where they might happen in September (oops, sorry NZ folks, I'm late!).

Everyone else, enjoy, you're on the right side of history, and we thank you for the good example you give us.

There's been of changes since last time:

  • British Columbia moved to permanent -07 on 2026-03-09, that is it will change to normal time in November

  • Alberta moved to permanent -06 on 2026-06-18, similar to BC above.

  • Canada’s Northwest Territories moved to permanent -06 on 2026-08-21, matching Alberta.

  • Manitoba moves to permanent -05 on 2026-10-31.

  • Morocco moves to permanent +00 on 2026-09-20.

  • Moldova has used EU transition times since 2022, but the tz database only noticed in 2026

This is my interpretation of the changes announced on the tzdata mailing list here:

https://lists.iana.org/hyperkitty/list/tz-announce@iana.org/latest

If the eastward trend continues, Canada should adopt country-wide "no daylight savings" rules by 2027, although there's actually no sign of the other provinces (Ontario, Québec and so on) currently running bills to change those rules just yet. Poor Canadians like me confused about time in their countries can refer to this section of Wikipedia for details:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time_in_Canada#By_province_and_territory

... and particularly the image featured there:

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Canada_time_zone_mapen.svg

It also seems like the US government finally adopt a permanent daylight saving change bill in 2026, as the "Sunshine protection act" pass the house in July:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunshine_Protection_Act

True to form, this was associated with absolutely ridiculous pressure from Donald Trump against republicans (his own party!) objecting to the change:

On July 14, 2026, the House passed a Sunshine Protection Act bill backed by President Trump. Nevertheless, the bill was opposed in the Senate by Republicans, including Senator Cotton. In response, on October 3, 2026, Trump shared a post on Truth Social urging Cotton to approve the bill, where he revealed Cotton's personal cellphone number and called on people to call him.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/trump-tom-cotton-daylight-saving-time

Given that the last time the US did a major change to the daylight savings policy (in 2005), Canada followed suit to stay in sync, it's quite possible Trump's mad dash might actually finish getting rid of DST in North America:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_Policy_Act_of_2005#Change_to_daylight_saving_time

items.title: Kentaro Hayashi: Testing Japanese IMEs on virtual desktops with virt-japanese-desktop
items.author: Kentaro Hayashi
items.content:
Japanese input method editors (IMEs) such as are essential for typing Japanese (yes, skk, anthy and more, but it's out-of-scope in this article). Testing them is a surprisingly fiddly job: an IME behaves differently depending on the desktop environment (GNOME, KDE, Xfce, Budgie), the input framework (ibus, fcitx5, uim), and the Wayland or X11 session. Setting up a fresh VM for every combination from scratch is slow and repetitive, and breaking your host's environment while experimenting is no fun.

is a small set of toy scripts that solves exactly this problem. It builds ready-to-use virtual machines - each with a desktop environment and a Japanese IME already installed and configured - so you can start typing Japanese within a minute of booting, and throw the whole thing away without any impact on your host.

A single command produces a qcow2 image that combines one of four desktops with one of three IMEs:

The one gap - - is a real technical limitation, not an oversight: Budgie runs the labwc compositor, which implements , while only speaks the older (KWin/Weston). On Budgie you use ibus-mozc or fcitx5-mozc instead.

All images come with the Japanese locale, fonts, and the time zone pre-configured, plus the SSH key of your choice. Input switching is wired up out of the box: or for your IMEs to enable it.

The core idea is that the images are stacked qcow2 overlay layers, one on top of another:

debian-sid-nocloud-amd64-daily.qcow2     ... base image you download
└─ unstable-japanese-template.qcow2      ... locale, fonts, user, SSH
   └─ unstable-<DE>-template.qcow2       ... a desktop environment
      └─ unstable-<DE>-<IME>.qcow2       ... desktop + IME, configured
         └─ unstable-<DE>-<IME>.workspace.qcow2 ... the image you test in

This makes both building and resetting fast. The first build downloads and customizes the base image and takes a while, but every later step only adds a thin overlay. When a test breaks the VM, you do not rebuild anything - you simply delete the top layer and recreate it. That is all it takes to return to a pristine state:

 /tmp/unstable-gnome-ibus-mozc.workspace.qcow2
make gnome-ibus-mozc

The images reference their backing files by , so you can move an entire stack anywhere you like as long as the images stay together.

The base system is Debian , and the repository is already added. That makes the project a convenient platform for testing not just the IME packages in sid but also the ones still being developed in - exactly what the project was built for.

The keyboard layout of the VM follows the layout of your host (read from , with a fallback chain to and finally ).

sudo apt install qemu-utils libguestfs-tools virt-install curl


curl  https://github.com/USERNAME.keys  pubkey.pub


make download


make gnome-ibus-mozc


./scripts/make-virsh-image.sh virt-gnome-ibus-mozc /tmp/unstable-gnome-ibus-mozc.workspace.qcow2

Log in as (password ) and press () to start typing Japanese. The VM is registered in libvirt, so you can manage it with or - handy for opening the SPICE console or restarting the machine after a test.

The project is still in the phase, and it is developed mainly to test Mozc and other IMEs across desktops and input frameworks.

If you regularly test Japanese IMEs - give it a try.
